rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to locate all six peaks and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing strongly retained compounds. The moderate temperature leaves room to explore temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

Injection 1 already attained the maximum CRF, so retain it as the benchmark. Shorten the gradient at unchanged temperature to seek a faster fully resolved method, using the substantial resolution margin.
Shorten the gradient by one grid step while keeping composition and temperature fixed. The current minimum resolution of 2.54 provides margin to reduce analysis time while preserving the maximum CRF.
Test the minimum gradient duration to establish the speed–resolution boundary; the first pair may fall below 1.5. Retain the fully resolved 4-minute gradient as the fallback.

Return to the shortest fully resolved gradient and raise temperature by one step to test whether elution can be accelerated without losing the critical first-pair separation. The 4-minute gradient at 40 C remains the maximum-CRF fallback.

The temperature increase reduced critical-pair resolution, so test whether cooling to 25 C can recover separation with the fastest gradient. Keep the fully resolved 4-minute, 40 C method as the benchmark.

Reduce the gradient slope at 25 C to lift the critical first-pair resolution above 1.5 while retaining the 2-minute ramp. The lower final organic fraction should modestly delay the last peak, but may yield a faster fully resolved method than the current benchmark.

Increase the final organic fraction by one grid step to accelerate the last peak and locate the critical-pair resolution boundary. Injection 7 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method if this steeper gradient drops resolution below 1.5.

Raise the starting organic fraction one step to reduce the ramp slope while preserving the stronger final solvent. This tests whether the first pair can regain full resolution without the last-peak delay seen at phi1 = 0.80.

Shift both gradient endpoints upward by 0.10, preserving the slope that gave full resolution in injection 9 while strengthening the final wash. This should accelerate the last peak, while testing whether earlier elution compromises the first pair.

Raise the starting organic fraction one grid step to shorten elution further while keeping the strongest final solvent. Monitor the first pair for loss of initial retention; injection 10 remains the fastest fully resolved benchmark.

Raise temperature one step to accelerate the last peak, using the improved minimum resolution of 1.77 as margin. Keep the gradient unchanged to isolate the temperature effect on the critical early pair.

Test one further increase in starting organic fraction to seek faster elution at the maximum CRF. The first peak is now near the gradient-outlet arrival time, so this run will check whether reduced initial retention compromises the early pair.

Restore phi0 to 0.30 and test the next temperature step to establish the thermal speed–resolution boundary. Injection 12 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF method if the first pair falls below 1.5.

Test whether a shallower ramp restores full first-pair resolution at 35 C, where the strongest-endpoint gradient narrowly failed. This explores a warmer maximum-CRF alternative; injection 12 remains the fastest fully resolved benchmark.

Lower the starting organic fraction to move the critical early pair into the gradient, where slope control may improve its separation. This tests a fully resolved 35 C alternative while retaining injection 12 as the fastest maximum-CRF benchmark.

Lower the final organic fraction one grid step to recover the small first-pair resolution deficit at 35 C. This should establish a fully resolved warmer alternative, although injection 12 remains the faster maximum-CRF benchmark.

Refine around the fastest fully resolved method by lowering both endpoints one step at the same temperature and slope. This tests whether greater initial retention provides useful first-pair resolution margin with only a small last-peak delay.

Reduce the final organic fraction one step relative to injection 12 to seek more critical-pair resolution margin with a modest time penalty. This refines a fast, fully resolved alternative while preserving injection 12 as the shortest demonstrated maximum-CRF method.

Test a lower starting organic fraction with the strongest endpoint to establish the low-phi0 boundary for full resolution in a fast method. This may provide an alternative with better initial retention; injection 12 remains the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF method.

Combine the cooler temperature with a slightly shallower ramp to seek greater first-pair resolution margin while keeping elution near 3 minutes. Injection 12 remains the fastest demonstrated method attaining the maximum CRF.

Test the remaining cooler neighbor of injection 18 to assess first-pair resolution margin with greater initial retention than phi0 = 0.30. The campaign has already reached the CRF ceiling; injection 12 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method.

Test a shallower neighboring gradient for additional first-pair resolution margin while keeping all peaks within a short analysis window. Retain injection 12 as the fastest demonstrated method with the maximum CRF.

Cool injection 23 by one grid step to test a fast alternative with greater critical-pair resolution margin. Injection 12 remains the fastest demonstrated fully resolved method, and the maximum campaign CRF is already secured.

Use the final injection to test a neighboring fast method with greater initial retention and an expected first-pair resolution margin. Retain injection 12 as the fastest demonstrated maximum-CRF method: phi0 0.30, phi1 0.95, tG 2 minutes, T 30 C.
